content: Postgraduate education, also referred to as graduate education in North America and sometimes described as quaternary education, involves pursuing advanced degrees or qualifications that require a prior Bachelor's degree. It is generally considered part of tertiary or higher education. In North America, this level of education is typically referred to as graduate school. The structure and organization of postgraduate education vary significantly across countries and even among institutions within the same country. In some traditional German educational systems, there is no legal distinction between undergraduate and postgraduate education. Instead, all academic programs are designed to culminate in a Master's degree, whether at an introductory (Bachelor's level) or advanced (Master's level). The Bologna Process aims to standardize and replace this system across Europe. Types of Postgraduate Qualifications Postgraduate qualifications can be broadly categorized into four main types: academic degrees, vocational degrees, academic certificates, and vocational certificates or diplomas. Degrees The term degree originates from the Latin deand gradus, meaning a step or stage, and was first used in the 13th century. Degrees signify progression from one academic level to another. Historical Context The concept of postgraduate education is rooted in the degree-awarding systems of medieval European universities, although higher education itself dates back to ancient civilizations such as Greece, China, India, and Africa. In medieval Europe, university studies typically required six years to earn a Bachelor's degree and up to twelve additional years for a Master's degree or doctorate. The initial six years focused on the faculty of arts, which included the seven liberal arts: arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, music theory, grammar, logic, and rhetoric, with a strong emphasis on logic. After obtaining a Bachelor of Arts degree, students could specialize in one of three faculties—law, medicine, or theology—to pursue a Master's or Doctor's degree. Theology was considered the most prestigious and challenging discipline. During this period, the titles of Master (magister) and Doctor were often used interchangeably, with regional preferences influencing their usage. For instance, Master was more common in Paris and its affiliated universities, while Doctor was favored in Bologna and its derivatives. Over time, theology's status as the highest discipline led to the doctorate being regarded as superior to the Master's degree. These advanced degrees primarily served as licenses to teach, with doctor derived from the Latin docere (to teach) and magister meaning master. Modern Hierarchy of Degrees In most English-speaking countries, the hierarchy of academic degrees is as follows: 1. Associate's Degree (or Foundation Degree in the UK) Typically a two-year program requiring 20 courses or 60 semester credit hours in the U.S. In the UK, a foundation degree is equivalent to 240 CATS credits or 120 ECTS credits. 2. Bachelor's Degrees (Undergraduate Degrees) Usually completed in three to four years, requiring 40 courses or 120 semester credit hours in the U.S. Some Bachelor's degrees, such as the Bachelor of Civil Law or Bachelor of Philosophy, are actually postgraduate degrees. In South Africa and other countries, a four-year program may confer an Honours Bachelor's degree, distinguishing it from a standard three-year Bachelor's degree. In France, the equivalent is the Licence degree, while in the Netherlands, the Hoger Beroeps Onderwijs (HBO) corresponds to a four-year Bachelor's program. 3. In North America, these programs often require a prior Bachelor's degree, followed by three to four years of specialized study. In other regions, professional education is typically integrated into undergraduate programs or post-university vocational training. 4. Master's Degrees (Postgraduate) Master's degrees can be categorized into taught programs (e.g., Master of Arts, Master of Science) and research-based programs (e.g., Master of Research, Master of Philosophy). In the UK, taught Master's degrees typically last one year and are worth 180 CATS credits (90 ECTS credits). Research-based Master's degrees, such as the MRes, also last one year but involve more extensive research. The MPhil often spans two years and may be awarded to students who do not complete a doctoral program. In some fields, such as clinical social work or library science in North America, the Master's degree is considered the terminal degree. 5. Doctorates (Postgraduate) Doctorates are divided into academic and professional categories. Academic doctorates include the PhD (Philosophiæ Doctor) and DSc (Scientiae Doctor), with the latter sometimes awarded in specific fields (e.g., Dr. sc. math for mathematics, Dr. sc. agr for agricultural sciences). In some European countries, doctorates are further divided into junior doctorates (e.g., PhD) and higher doctorates (e.g., DSc), which are typically awarded to distinguished scholars. In the U.S., there is little distinction between a PhD and a DSc. In the UK, PhD degrees are often equivalent to 540 CATS credits (270 ECTS credits), although this is not universally standardized. Historically, the Master's degree was the primary postgraduate qualification in the UK and its former colonies. However, the adoption of the European model in the 19th century led to the introduction of doctorates in the U.S., a practice that later spread to the UK. Honorary Degrees Universities often confer honorary degrees, typically at the postgraduate level, to individuals who have made significant contributions to fields such as the arts, politics, business, or academia. Recipients of honorary degrees generally do not use the associated titles or post-nominal letters (e.g., Dr). Non-Degree Qualifications Postgraduate education also includes non-degree qualifications such as postgraduate certificates and diplomas. These credentials are generally considered lower than degrees and may serve as stepping stones toward a degree, specialized career training, or recognition in a narrowly focused area of study.
